results.title: Meta Analysis for Binary Outcome in SPSS - Explained, Example
results.content: # Meta Analysis for Binary Outcome in SPSS. Discover **Meta Analysis for Binary Outcome in SPSS**! Meta-analysis of binary outcomes is a crucial tool in evidence-based medicine, enabling researchers to combine effect sizes from multiple studies to determine the overall treatment effect for dichotomous (yes/no) variables. Binary meta-analysis refers to the statistical synthesis of results from studies with dichotomous outcomes, such as event/no-event, success/failure, or improved/not improved. In addition to binary outcomes, meta-analysis can be applied to other data types depending on the study design and reported results. * **Continuous Outcome Meta-Analysis**: Used when studies report means and standard deviations (e.g., blood pressure, symptom scores). * **Meta-Regression:** Meta-regression examines whether study-level variables (e.g., sample size, year, dosage) explain variation in effect sizes. When to Use Meta-Analysis of Binary Outcomes? Binary meta-analysis is used when studies report results in binary format. What Effect Size for Binary Outcome in Meta Analysis? In SPSS, you can choose from several effect sizes for binary outcome meta-analysis. What is the Difference Between Fixed and Random effects in Meta Analysis of Binary outcomes? What Estimator Type of Meta Analysis of Binary Outcome? **Best Choice**: For most binary outcome meta-analyses, use **REML** for more stable estimates of heterogeneity and pooled effects. Heterogeneity in Meta Analysis of Binary Outcome. What is Publication Bias in Meta Analysis of Binary Outcome? What is Used for a Funnel and Forest Plot in Meta Analysis of Binary Outcome? SPSS generates both plots automatically in binary meta-analysis using the appropriate chart options. What Are the Assumptions of Meta-Analysis for Binary Outcome? An Example for Meta Analysis for Binary Outcome. The researcher converts event data into log odds ratios and performs a meta-analysis using the random-effects model. How to Perform Meta Analysis for Binary in SPSS. ## **Step by Step: Running Meta-Analysis in SPSS Statistics**. In SPSS version 28 and higher, you can directly conduct meta-analysis for binary outcomes using the native interface. To perform binary meta-analysis in SPSS:. STEP**: Go to `Analyze` → `Meta Analysis` → `Binary Outcome`. How to Interpret SPSS Output of Binary Meta Analysis. Once the analysis is complete, SPSS generates a detailed output including pooled effect estimates, confidence intervals, heterogeneity indices, and plots.

results.title: Measures of effect size
results.content: Measures of effect size William Roberts Psychology Department Thompson Rivers University wlroberts@tru.ca 25 February 2013 In writing term papers, it is important to estimate the extent to which various possible causal factors are related to the outcome that interests you. The most important measures of effect size are r, the correlation coefficient, and R², the proportion of total variability explained. The software available at http://www.tru.ca/faculty/wlroberts/#effect size and at http://sourceforge.net/projects/behavioraldata/files/ can convert other measures of effect size (below) to R², so that R² can serve as a common metric across studies. Given a correlation and a sample size, the calculator at http://www.tru.ca/faculty/wlroberts/r_confidence_interval.exe will return the 95% confidence interval, as well as the significance (p-value) of the correlation, and the critical values for r at various levels of alpha (.10, .05, .01, and .001) in a sample of the size given. If a published table of correlations seems to contain fewer significant findings than one might expect, you can assess the omnibus null hypothesis using the calculator at http://www.tru.ca/faculty/wlroberts/omnibus.exe.

results.title: Correlated Bivariate Continuous and Binary Outcomes: Issues and Applications - PMC
results.content: We present a new multivariate model to analyze binary and continuous correlated outcomes using a latent variable. All the settings produced identical point estimates (MLEs) of the parameters, despite the model used to fit the data, the effect size of the covariate or the correlation level between the two outcomes. Tables I, II and III present the ratio of the MSE of the multivariate models (factorization model, latent variable model and GEE) to the univariate model in different settings depending on the effect size of the shared covariate and correlation level between the outcomes. Mean square errors (MSE) from the simulation study with no effect of the shared covariate (*β**b*1 = 0) on the binary outcome and a small effect on the continuous outcome (*β**c*1 = 2; 1/3 of a SD): ratio of the MSE of the multivariate models (factorization model(24), latent variable model(25) and GEE(18)) to the univariate model(23). Mean square errors (MSE) from the simulation study with small effect of the shared covariate (*β**b*1 = 0:2; 1/5 of a SD) on the binary outcome and a small effect on the continuous outcome (*β**c*1 = 2; 1/3 of a SD): ratio of the MSE of the multivariate models (factorization model(24), latent variable model(25) and GEE(18)) to the univariate model(23). Mean square errors (MSE) from the simulation study with large effect of the shared covariate (*β**b*1 = 1; 1 SD) on the binary outcome and a large effect on the continuous outcome (*β**c*1 = 6; 1 SD): ratio of the MSE of the multivariate models (factorization model(24), latent variable model(25) and GEE(18)) to the univariate model(23). However, the estimate of treatment effect for the binary outcome, loss of at least three lines of vision at 1 year, was smaller in the latent variable model (Table V). In contrast to the factorization approach, the latent variable model presented is easily extended to several continuous and/or several binary outcomes by including additional latent variables as long as the outocomes are positively correlated.
